text: lecular-weight heparins may be as safe and effective as warfarin when given for 3 months; they may be more effective than con- tinued warfarin in patients with recurrence during warfarin therapy.72 They may also be more effective than warfarin as initial therapy in patients with cancer,73 and are recommended56 for the first 3 to 6 months of long-term anticoagulant therapy in such patients. Use of lower-inten- sity warfarin regimens has been tried for extended proph- ylaxis, and may reduce the risk of recurrence compared with no therapy.74 However, a study75 comparing low- and high-intensity regimens found that the lower intensity reg- imen was less effective and did not reduce the risk of bleeding. Subcutaneous idraparinux, a factor Xa inhibitor, has also been tried,76 but may cause more bleeding than standard therapy when given for extended periods.77 In pa- tients who have contra-indications to anticoagulation or in whom thrombosis recurs despite anticoagulation, insertion of a vena caval filter may be appropriate. The use of filters with anticoagulation has also been investigated.78 Al- though the incidence of pulmonary embolism was reduced during the first 12 days, no effect on mortality was shown at 2 years. Therapy with thrombolytics such as streptokinase is gen- erally reserved for very extensive thrombosis. A systemat- ic review79 showed no effect on mortality in patients with DVT and the main advantages are continued venous pat- ency and reduced incidence of post-phlebitic syndrome. There may be a small risk of increased bleeding. Since thrombolytic activity fades when infusion stops, heparin followed by oral anticoagulation is given to prevent re-oc- clusion. Minor pulmonary embolism is treated with heparin or low- molecular-weight heparin and oral anticoagulants as de- scribed for DVT (above).6,80-85 Fondaparinux may be an alternative to heparin.83,84,86 For more severe pulmonary embolism the initial bolus dose of heparin may be dou- bled. An initial dose of unfractionated heparin may also be given before treatment with low-molecular-weight heparins.6 Acute massive pulmonary embolism with major haemodynamic disturbance may be treated initially with thrombolytic therapy;5,6,83,84 surgical methods such Cardiovascular Drugs 1191 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) as embolectomy or percutaneous catheter fragmentation may be preferred in some patients.83,84,87,88 Streptokinase, urokinase, and alteplase have all been shown to accelerate the lysis of pulmonary emboli and to decrease pulmonary vascular obstruction.
